content: Hepatitis C is a liver disease caused by the hepatitis C virus (HCV). Globally, approximately 150 million people are chronically infected with HCV, and an additional three to four million new infections occur annually. Chronic hepatitis C is a major contributor to liver-related morbidity and mortality. Between 5% and 20% of individuals with chronic HCV infection develop liver cirrhosis, which significantly increases the risk of hepatocellular carcinoma and liver failure. Until 2011, the standard treatment for chronic hepatitis C involved a combination of pegylated interferon-alpha (peginterferon) and ribavirin. In 2011, first-generation direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) were introduced for use in combination with peginterferon and ribavirin, specifically for treating HCV genotype 1 infections. Nitazoxanide, an antiviral drug with broad-spectrum activity, has been proposed as a potential alternative or adjunct to standard treatments for HCV. The objective of this review was to evaluate the benefits and harms of nitazoxanide in individuals with chronic HCV infection. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Hepato-Biliary Group Controlled Trials Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, LILACS, and the Science Citation Index EXPANDED, covering studies up to April 2013. Additional searches were performed in ClinicalTrials.gov and the World Health Organization's International Clinical Trials Registry Platform for registered trials, both completed and ongoing. The review included randomized clinical trials comparing nitazoxanide with placebo, no intervention, or other treatments in patients with chronic HCV. Trials were eligible if they allowed co-interventions, such as standard treatment, provided these were administered equally across all intervention groups. Data extraction and risk of bias assessments were conducted independently by two reviewers. Statistical analyses were performed using both fixed-effect and random-effects models, and the quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE system. Seven randomized clinical trials involving 538 participants with chronic HCV (genotype 1 or 4) were included. All participants were adults aged 18 years or older. All trials were determined to have a high risk of bias. Six of the seven trials included antiviral co-interventions administered equally across groups. Only one trial, which compared nitazoxanide plus peginterferon and ribavirin to no intervention plus peginterferon and ribavirin, reported no deaths from any cause or from chronic hepatitis C (100 participants; very low-quality evidence). The effect of nitazoxanide on adverse events was uncertain. In four trials, 21% of participants in the nitazoxanide group experienced adverse events compared to 20% in the placebo or no-intervention group (risk ratio [RR] 1.10; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.71 to 1.71; I² = 65%; very low-quality evidence). Nitazoxanide reduced the risk of failure to achieve a sustained virological response (SVR) compared to placebo or no intervention (55% vs. 64%; RR 0.85; 95% CI 0.75 to 0.97; I² = 0%; seven trials; low-quality evidence). It also reduced the risk of failure to achieve a virological end-of-treatment response (43% vs. 53%; RR 0.81; 95% CI 0.69 to 0.96; I² = 46%; seven trials; low-quality evidence). Trial sequential analysis supported the findings for SVR but not for virological end-of-treatment response. Nitazoxanide did not significantly improve alanine aminotransferase (ALT) or aspartate aminotransferase (AST) serum levels compared to placebo or no intervention (54% vs. 49%; RR 1.09; 95% CI 0.84 to 1.42; I² = 0%; three trials; very low-quality evidence). None of the included trials assessed the effects of nitazoxanide on morbidity or quality of life. Histological changes were reported in only three participants from a subset of 13 individuals in a long-term follow-up trial. The authors concluded that there is very low-quality or no evidence regarding the effects of nitazoxanide on clinically relevant outcomes, such as all-cause mortality, HCV-related mortality, morbidity, and adverse events in patients with chronic HCV genotype 1 or 4. The findings regarding ALT and AST levels were inconclusive. While nitazoxanide may have an effect on SVR and virological end-of-treatment response, these results are potentially influenced by systematic errors due to the high risk of bias in the included trials. Only the beneficial effect on SVR was supported by trial sequential analysis, while the findings for virological end-of-treatment response may be due to random error. No data were available on the effects of nitazoxanide in patients with HCV genotypes 2 or 3. Further randomized clinical trials with low risk of bias are needed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of nitazoxanide for chronic hepatitis C.
